summary: Addresses the growth of RTCP reception reports when several RTP streams are sent in one session, since each source normally reports on every other source. It defines a way to group reception statistics and other feedback so the volume grows with the number of endpoints, not streams. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: If every person in a room had to write a report about every other person, there would be mountains of paper. This document lets people share reports in groups so there is far less to write.

questions: how to reduce rtcp reports with many ssrcs
what is an rtcp reporting group
what is the rtcp rgrs packet
how to reduce rtcp overhead with many ssrcs
subtitle: Lets co-located RTP sources share one set of RTCP reception reports instead of each reporting on everyone.

tldr.problem: When one RTP session carries many streams, every SSRC must send RTCP reception reports about every other SSRC, so report traffic grows with the number of SSRCs rather than the number of endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: SSRCs on the same endpoint that see identical network conditions form a Reporting Group. One or more reporting sources send the reports for the group, and the other members send a small RGRS packet saying who reports for them.
tldr.outcome: RTCP overhead drops sharply with no loss of useful information. The RFC's worked example shows the normal reporting interval being about 9 times longer than with groups. Observers unaware of the extension may misread the empty reports.

facts.label: Worked example saving
facts.value: reporting interval about 9 times longer without groups

today: RFC 8861 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and the metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: The Reporting Overhead Problem
sections.content:
An RTP session can carry many streams, for example a participant with several cameras, or audio and video multiplexed together. Each stream has a synchronization source (SSRC), and the base rules in RFC 3550 say every SSRC sends sender or receiver reports about every other SSRC.

The RFC gives an example: ten participants each sending three media sources makes 30 SSRCs, and each of the 30 sends an RTCP report packet per interval covering all the others. But the three SSRCs of one participant are usually co-located and see identical reception quality, so two-thirds of those reports could be suppressed. The saved bandwidth lets the remaining reports go out more often within the same RTCP bandwidth fraction.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in a big class had to write a note about every classmate, the teacher would drown in notes. Many of the notes would say exactly the same thing.

sections.title: How a Reporting Group Works
sections.content:
An RTCP Reporting Group is a set of SSRCs co-located at a single endpoint (an end host or a middlebox) that see identical network conditions. An endpoint MAY group SSRCs only if they report on traffic received at the same interface. SSRCs with different views of the network MUST NOT share a group.

The endpoint picks one or more reporting sources. A reporting source sends the SR/RR reception reports for the whole group and MUST suppress reports about other members, reporting only on remote SSRCs. The other members suppress their reception reports and send an RGRS packet instead. If the session has many remote SSRCs, a group MAY use more than one reporting source, but their sets of remote SSRCs MUST NOT overlap.

A group made of only one local SSRC is not allowed, unless more SSRCs are expected to join later. If a reporting source leaves, the remaining members MUST hand its reporting to another reporting source, choose a new one, or disband the group and go back to normal reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: The family picks a spokesperson. The spokesperson writes the report, and everyone else just writes a note saying who the spokesperson is.

sections.title: The RGRP Item and RGRS Packet
sections.content:
Two new pieces of RTCP identify groups. The RGRP SDES item names the group. It has the same syntax as the CNAME item, with item type 11 instead of 1, and the same uniqueness and privacy concerns. Reporting sources MUST send it in every compound RTCP packet that carries an SR or RR, and its value MUST stay stable for the life of the group even if SSRCs change.

The RGRS packet (Reporting Group Reporting Sources) has packet type 212. It carries the sender's SSRC and a list of reporting source SSRCs, with the Source Count field giving the number of entries. It MUST contain at least one, so the length field is always 2 or greater. Every non-reporting member MUST include one in each compound RTCP packet where it sends an RR or SR. This lets others tell a silent group member apart from a receiver that really is receiving nothing. If there are more reporting sources than fit, members rotate through them round-robin.

Mixers and translators that forward group reports MUST also forward the RGRP items and RGRS packets, and MUST rewrite SSRCs in them if they rewrite SSRCs elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The group gets a name tag (RGRP). Members who are not the spokesperson carry a card (RGRS) that points to the spokesperson.

sections.title: Feedback, Extended Reports and Middleboxes
sections.content:
With the RTP/AVPF profile, each group member SHOULD still send its own rapid feedback and codec control messages, because who sent a message can matter. For instance, a video sender may treat loss feedback from an audio receiver as less urgent. An endpoint MAY send all feedback from the reporting source if the sender is not semantically important. AVPF timing is per SSRC, so one SSRC sending everything limits the feedback rate.

For RTCP XR packets, the reporting source is RECOMMENDED to send them, so they line up in time with the report blocks. Media-specific XR blocks MUST come from the SSRC they relate to.

Middleboxes can use groups only for their own SSRCs. A middlebox with no SSRC of its own cannot use the extension, and it cannot group the RTCP of streams it merely forwards.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes it matters who is talking, so members can still speak up for themselves. The spokesperson only handles the routine reports.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content:
Support is announced with the SDP attribute a=rtcp-rgrp, a property attribute that takes no value. A party that proposes it SHALL itself be able to receive Reporting Groups.

In offer/answer (RFC 3264), an offerer that supports the extension MUST include the attribute, and an answerer that supports it MAY include it in reply and MAY then send group extensions. If the answer contains the attribute but the offer did not, the offerer MUST reject the call. If the answer omits it, the offerer MUST NOT send the extensions. In declarative uses such as RTSP or SAP, the attribute means the participant MAY use groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the shortcut, both sides check that the other understands it. If one side does not, they go back to the long way.

sections.title: Bandwidth Savings and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC works an example of two endpoints, each with a hundred sources, of which eight each are sending. Baseline RTCP is 200 SDES packets, 184 RR packets and 16 SR packets, about 6.5 KB per interval. Under the original rules, report blocks add about 76 KB per interval, which is 92% of RTCP traffic. With Reporting Groups, reports shrink to about 0.4 KB, plus about 2.4 KB for RGRP items and RGRS packets. The unmodified reporting interval is approximately 9 times longer than with groups.

The catch is compatibility. To observers who do not know about groups, non-reporting members look like receivers that see a sender not at all. A sender using RTCP for congestion control might wrongly conclude there is complete congestion collapse. The RFC notes that spotting this needs fairly sophisticated analysis and that reports in large conferences can be round-robined anyway, so it calls the real-world impact unclear.
sections.plainLanguage: With the shortcut, a mountain of paperwork shrinks to a small pile. The risk is that someone who has not heard of the shortcut might think the quiet family members have vanished.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550 and RFC 8108 apply, plus those of AVPF and XR when used. Without integrity protection, an attacker can alter the RGRP item or RGRS packet, causing parsing failure, packets being discarded, or inconsistent group information. The RFC judges these to be limited-impact attacks, since modifying the reports themselves would be at least as effective.

Integrity and source authentication SHOULD be applied, for example with SRTP (RFC 3711). For privacy, a long-term stable or predictable group identifier could be used to track an endpoint, so it is RECOMMENDED to generate it as a short-term persistent value following the CNAME rules in RFC 7022.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bully scribbles on the name tags, the reports get confusing or thrown away. A lock on the packets stops that, and name tags should change often so nobody can follow you around by one.

fields.desc: Number of reporting source SSRCs in the packet; at least one.

fields.desc: Length in 32-bit words minus one; always 2 or greater.
